title: Things Used to Be Different -- Twenty Years of This Industry
desc: Used to and would, for the way the job worked before everything moved online. Key expressions: to phase out, legacy system, paper trail, turnaround, fleet, ground staff, overhaul, back then, to take for granted, old-school, to rely on, to die out. Structure: used to for states and habits that are over, would for actions that repeated -- and why would never works with be, have or know.
vocab: To phase out
to stop using something gradually, over a period of time
They phased out the paper contract over about three years.
Legacy system
an old computer system that a company still uses
Two of the four countries are still on the legacy system.
Paper trail
the written record that shows what happened and who decided it
Everybody used to know where the paper trail was.
Turnaround
the time an aircraft spends on the ground between two flights
The turnaround used to be an hour, and now it is forty minutes.
Fleet
all the aircraft that an airline owns or operates
When I started, the fleet used to be half the size it is now.
Ground staff
the people who work at the airport, not on board the aircraft
The ground staff would call us directly when a group was delayed.
Overhaul
a complete change or repair of a system
The reporting system needs an overhaul, not another workaround.
Back then
at that time in the past
Back then, a contract used to take three weeks to arrive.
To take for granted
to stop noticing how valuable something is
We used to take that weekly visit for granted.
Old-school
done in the traditional way, before the new methods
He is old-school, and his clients have never left him.
To rely on
to depend on something or somebody to work properly
We used to rely on the ground staff for what the system did not have.
To die out
to slowly disappear completely
That habit died out quietly, and no system replaced it.

paras: There is a photograph on the wall of the São Paulo office, taken about twenty years ago. It shows shelves full of folders, one for every corporate client. Back then, contracts used to arrive on paper: a courier would bring them twice a week and somebody would file them by hand.

The job used to be physical in a way that is difficult to explain now. If a client called about a fare, the account manager would walk to the shelf, open the folder and read the answer out loud. It was slow. It was also completely transparent: everybody knew where the paper trail was.

Other things were different too. The fleet used to be about half the size it is today, the turnaround used to be an hour instead of forty minutes, and account managers used to rely on the ground staff for information that no system had. The company phased out the paper contract over about three years, and two countries are still on the legacy system that replaced it, which is why the reporting needs an overhaul and not another workaround.

Nobody is nostalgic about the paper, and nobody wants the courier back. What the old-school veterans miss is a habit the shelf forced on them: they would open the whole folder twice a week, problem or no problem, and see the client as a whole. That habit died out quietly and nothing replaced it. Most people used to take it for granted, which is exactly why nobody noticed it going.
quiz: Why does the text say "contracts used to arrive on paper" instead of "contracts arrived on paper"?
Because used to signals that it was the normal state and it is over.
Because it is still true today.
"The fleet used to be half the size it is now." Could you say "the fleet would be half the size"?
Yes, they mean the same thing.
No, because be is a state, and would only works for repeated actions.
No, because the fleet is not a person.
What does the text say the veterans actually miss?
The courier who came twice a week.
The habit of looking at the whole client twice a week.
The text says the company "phased out" the paper contract. What does that mean?
It stopped on one day, by decision.
It was stopped gradually, over a period of time.

tip.title: Used To and Would
tip.intro: Two ways of saying that something was normal in the past and is not any more. They overlap most of the time -- and there is exactly one situation where only one of them works.
rows: It was the normal state of things and it is not any more. Works for habits and for states.

"Contracts used to arrive on paper."
"The fleet used to be smaller."
A repeated action in the past. Warmer and more narrative — this is the storytelling one.
"A courier would bring them twice a week."
Would does not work for states. be, have, know, live, own, believe take only used to.

"I used to have thirty accounts."
NOT "I would have thirty accounts."
The d disappears after did: did not use to, did you use to.

"I did not use to travel every week."
"Did you use to work in tourism?"
Set the scene with used to, then switch to would for the actions that repeated. That is how a native narrates twenty years.
"Contracts used to arrive on paper. A courier would bring them, and we would file them by hand."
tip.note: One test decides it: is this an action that repeated, or a state that was true? If it is a state, only used to works.

blanks: Contracts
used to arrive
Hint: it was the normal state and it is over -- used to plus the base verb
Contracts used to arrive on paper, twice a week.
on paper, twice a week.
A courier
would bring
Hint: a repeated action, so the storytelling form works here
A courier would bring them to the office every Tuesday and Friday.
them to the office every Tuesday and Friday.
The fleet
used to be
Hint: be is a state, and only one of the two forms works with states
The fleet used to be half the size it is now.
half the size it is now.
Did you use to
Hint: after did, the d disappears
Did you use to work in tourism before this?
work in tourism before this?
We
used to have
Hint: have is a state, so would does not work
We used to have a folder on the shelf for every client.
a folder on the shelf for every client.
The ground staff
would call
Hint: something that happened again and again
The ground staff would call us directly when a group was delayed.
us directly when a group was delayed.

order.intro: Listen to the summary of the conversation with the veteran from operations, then put the steps in the correct order.
items: Renato says that the photograph on the wall shows the office as it used to be twenty years ago.
Rosa asks how the contracts used to arrive before the portal existed.
Renato explains that a courier would bring them twice a week and that everything was filed by hand.
Rosa asks what he misses most about that way of working.
Renato answers that he does not miss the paper, but he misses the habit of looking at the whole client twice a week.

speech: Back then, contracts used to arrive on paper.
We would file every contract by hand.
Did you use to work in tourism before this?
That habit died out, and no system replaced it.
We used to visit every week, and today we answer much faster.

quiz.intro: A younger colleague is asking about the old days, and a long-standing client says the service has changed. Choose the best thing to say.
items: He asks how contracts arrived before the portal. You say:
Contracts use to arrive on paper.
Contracts used to arrive on paper, twice a week.
Contracts would be on paper, twice a week.
You want to describe something that happened again and again. You say:
A courier would bring them every Tuesday and Friday.
A courier used to bringing them every Tuesday and Friday.
A courier brings them every Tuesday and Friday.
You want to say the fleet was smaller. You say:
The fleet would be half the size it is now.
The fleet used to be half the size it is now.
The fleet use to be half the size it is now.
You want to ask about his previous career. You ask:
Did you used to work in tourism?
Did you use to work in tourism before this?
Used you to work in tourism?
A client says the service is not what it used to be. The best first answer is:
That is not true, our service is better than ever.
You are right, everything is worse now.
You are right about one thing: we used to visit every week. Today we answer much faster, and I would like to bring the visit back for you.

think: Record about two minutes about your own career for somebody who was not there. Say where you started, what a normal week used to be, one thing you would do every week that you no longer do, one habit that died out in this industry, and one thing that is genuinely better today. Use used to for the states and would for the actions that repeated.
survival: Back then, contracts used to arrive on paper.
We would file every contract by hand.
Did you use to work in tourism before this?
That habit died out, and no system replaced it.
We used to visit every week, and today we answer much faster.
